analysis.title: The $20 Trillion AI Crash: Tech Breaks, Credit Cracks, And The Canaries Are Screaming
key_insights: TS Lombard wargames an AI investment bust and models a roughly $20 trillion US equity market cap wipeout, $125-190 billion of AI-related credit losses and a US recession.

The modelled recession is relatively mild, comparable to 1990 or 2001 rather than 2008. The direct AI investment reversal could subtract about 2 percentage points from US GDP, cushioned by healthy private-sector balance sheets and room for Fed easing.
The semiconductor index is breaking below the trading range in place since May and trading down to its 200-day moving average. Semiconductor volatility is also spiking.

Estimates cited say annual AI revenues must reach $2.5-3 trillion by 2030 to justify the spending, roughly 14 times current levels. Much of the ecosystem's revenue reflects recycled capex rather than demand from outside customers.
TS Lombard expects about $700 billion of new AI-related bond issuance in 2027, including $400 billion from hyperscalers. Estimates of hidden liabilities across the ecosystem are $1.5-2 trillion.
AI capex does not need to fall for financial stress to emerge, it only needs to grow more slowly, because revenue backlogs, borrowing and investment commitments depend on continued expansion.
The crash scenario assumes the S&P 500 falls 30%, with technology down 40% and other sectors down 20%. Technology is roughly 40% of the US stock market.
The biggest credit vulnerabilities are neoclouds, leveraged infrastructure developers and private credit rather than the cash-rich hyperscalers.
KOSPI has fallen sharply from its highs, led by semiconductor heavyweights. The index trades well below its 200-day moving average and the 21-day average has crossed below the 200-day.
Korea and Taiwan have benefited disproportionately from AI-linked exports, which makes both vulnerable if US technology spending slows.

In the crash scenario TS Lombard expects government bonds to benefit as the demand shock pushes growth, inflation and yields lower. International equities could eventually outperform the US, though Korea and Taiwan stay vulnerable. Positioning too early could be costly.

sector_views.rationale: Scenario assumes technology stocks fall 40% in an AI crash, and the semiconductor index is already breaking below its range since May and testing its 200-day average.
An AI-driven demand shock would push growth, inflation and yields lower, benefiting government bonds.

tension_points.bull_case: AI investment continues to grow and the hyperscalers are cash-rich, so the financing structure holds.
tension_points.bear_case: Revenue must reach $2.5-3 trillion by 2030, about 14 times current levels, while revenue is partly recycled capex and financing relies more on external debt. Even slower capex growth could destabilize financing.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A deceleration in AI capex growth, which TS Lombard says is enough to destabilize the financing structure.
